title: Queueing Theory and Reserved GPU SLO Planning with Aurora Health
summary: Deep technical discussion focusing on autoscaling and capacity planning for a mixed latency-throughput workload. Main topics: modeling queueing for bursty traffic, dimensioning reserved GPU pools, KV cache warmup behavior, batching tradeoffs for low P95 latency, quantization impacts, and on-prem/VPC networking constraints. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with traffic replay and a sizing worksheet; Redwood to share benchmark templates and reserved GPU cost estimates.
topics: queueing theory / M/M/c vs M/G/1 approximations
reserved GPU sizing and concurrency planning
KV cache warmup, prefix caching and TTLs
batching windows vs p95 latency tradeoffs

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-03 15:00 PDT
Duration: 1:02:00
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (CTO - Aurora Health), Eric Zhao (ML Eng), Monica Reyes (Infra)
Link to shared deck: (redwood) https://redwood.internal/decks/aurora-q3-scaling (note: shared after call)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We got about an hour — Lina and I will walk through queueing and sizing, and then we want to understand your traffic patterns. Priya, quick intro?
[00:12] Priya: Yep, thanks. We run a mix of interactive clinician prompts and nightly batch summaries. Interactive traffic is spiky — morning shift, charting bursts, QPS jumps for 10-15 minutes. P95 SLA target is 250 milliseconds for interactive queries.
[00:28] Lina: Got it. That combination — steady batch plus bursty interactive — is exactly where reserved pools and shaping policies matter. We'll talk about a hybrid model: reserved GPUs for baseline, burst queue (shared) for peaks.
[00:44] Eric: Quick note: our infra team prefers VPC-only flows, on-prem for PHI. We need to make sure anything that keeps data in our VPC is possible.
[00:52] Samir: Absolutely — we have Redwood Private options and VPC connectors. We'll call out network egress and KMS nuances later.

[01:20] Lina: First principle — model the arrival process. For short interactive calls it's not exactly Poisson, but Poisson (M/M/c) is a useful upper bound for tail estimates. For heavy-tailed bursts we look at M/G/1 approximations or use empirical replay.
[01:45] Priya: Can you explain the practical difference? I mean, we don't want to overprovision but also can't have P95 spikes.
[01:53] Lina: Sure. Poisson assumptions smooths things; it underestimates peaks if traffic is correlated. So for safety we take a burst factor — e.g., 2.5x observed steady concurrency in the peak minute — and then run simulations with your actual traces. Traffic replay is key.

[02:30] Eric: How do KV caches play into this? We noticed long tails when caches cold for certain prefixes.
[02:36] Lina: KV cache warmup is often the biggest cause of transient P95 spikes. If your workload has repeated prefixes per clinician session the prefix cache hit-rate can be >90% after warmup. But cold-starts are painful — you either pre-warm commonly used prefixes on scale-up or you accept higher tails for first N minutes.
[02:58] Monica: Pre-warming sounds expensive for large model pools. Any heuristics?
[03:03] Lina: Heuristics: keep a small LRU of the top 5% prefixes in memory across the reserved pool; when you scale up, populate new instances with those keys from a central shared cache (or persistent in-memory snapshot). Also set TTLs to avoid thrash. We'll share our cache-warmup template.

[03:30] Samir: On reserved GPU sizing — simple back-of-envelope: required_concurrency = (peak_qps * avg_tokens_per_request / tokens_per_second_per_gpu) * safety_factor. But tokens_per_second depends on model size, quantization, and kernel selection.
[03:58] Priya: Walk that back with numbers — say peak 40 qps, avg 120 tokens, model is 7B.
[04:05] Lina: For a quantized 7B on A100-like perf, assume ~600 tokens/sec per GPU at inference config X (these are examples, we'll bench). So concurrency = (40 * 120) / 600 = 8 GPUs worth of concurrency; safety_factor 1.5 -> 12 logical concurrency slots, which maps to how many reserved workers you need given your worker concurrency (e.g., 2 async streams per GPU).
[04:30] Eric: So reserved "8 GPUs" vs "12" — what's the difference in latency?
[04:36] Lina: More pool capacity reduces queueing delay and keeps batching windows small; it also lets per-request batching remain small which is better for low-latency SLOs.

[05:10] Samir: Another lever is batching window tuning. If you open windows longer you improve throughput but increase P95. For interactive mode we typically use adaptive batching with max latency cap (e.g., 50ms ceiling).
[05:28] Priya: We've seen long queue times during lunch-tasks transitions — how would shaping help?
[05:35] Lina: Use token-bucket based burst controllers to limit peak admission to the shared pool, funneling excess into delayed queues or fallback smaller models. You can also prioritize clinician-facing queries over analytics background jobs with priority queues.

[06:10] Monica: On quantization — how much latency improvement are we realistically getting? And any tradeoffs with accuracy/regulatory?
[06:18] Lina: 4-bit PTQ or QAT variants can reduce model latency by 20-40% depending on kernel efficiency. But quant impacts logits subtly; for clinical tasks you want a QAT step and evals tied to your prompt sets. Redwood Optimize runs quality regressions on your prompt set.

[06:55] Samir: Let's talk queueing models briefly — FIFO is simplest but priority queues + admission control give better SLO for critical traffic. For rigorous planning we run an M/M/c baseline and then Monte Carlo traces from your replay to estimate tail probability.
[07:20] Eric: Do you support delayed warm pools? Like keep N warm but idle, then spin up extra on sustained load?
[07:27] Lina: Yes — reserved for baseline, a warm 'standing by' buffer for sub-minute spikes, then cold burst to shared GPUs. Warm buffers reduce cold-KV hits. There is cost trade-off.

[08:05] Priya: Networking — if we use Redwood Private inside our VPC, does the cache traffic flow inside the VPC?
[08:12] Samir: Yes, for Private deployments the KV cache and model-serving plane can be inside the VPC. We still need to coordinate KMS for key access and ensure no public egress for PHI. Monica, this will depend on your subnet/NAT config.

[08:44] Monica: Our egress links have quota during backups, could that throttle model warmups?
[08:48] Lina: Potentially if you pre-warm from object storage cross-region. Best is to use a regional warm snapshot in local ephemeral storage or shared in-memory store inside VPC. We'll outline patterns.

[09:30] Samir: We should step through a sample sizing scenario with your trace. Lina, you want to walk through the worksheet?
[09:36] Lina: Yup. (screen share) Worksheet columns: minute, observed_qps, avg_tokens, 95th_tokens, concurrency_estimate, required_gpus_raw, safety_factor, recommended_reserved. We prefer to recommend a tiered plan: reserved baseline for 90% of minutes, warm buffer for top 5%, burst for headroom.

[10:10] Priya: That tiering makes sense. How do we set the safety factor?
[10:14] Lina: Depends on tolerance for cost vs risk. For clinical interactive we recommend 1.5x; for internal analytics maybe 1.2x. Also include warmup penalty for kv-cold minutes — treat those minutes as higher token cost.

[11:00] Eric: If we use smaller batching windows, do we lose the benefit of kernel batching and vectorization?
[11:07] Lina: Some yes. The runtime uses continuous batching; more workers at lower batch sizes still benefit because they fill micro-batches across in-flight requests. The sweet spot is per-model and per-hardware; that's why we bench.

[11:40] Samir: On the pilot — we'll do three bench profiles: 1) Low-latency (50ms batching cap), 2) Balanced (100ms cap), 3) Throughput (batch aggressively). Each profile will run a replay of your trace and produce P50/P95/P99, token cost, and recommended reserved size.

[12:10] Priya: How long do we need the replay to be representative? We can give 7 days but do we simulated long tails?
[12:18] Lina: 7 days is ideal. We'll also do stress tests where we inject sustained 3-5x peaks for burst resilience.

[12:42] Eric: Any notes on eviction policies for KV cache? LRU is default but for clinical prefixes we might want LFU or sticky retention for session keys.
[12:51] Lina: Exactly — sticky retention for session-based prefixes helps. Also shard keys by clinician-id to avoid hotspots on single node. We'll provide config examples in the cache template.

[13:20] Monica: What about fallback model strategies if the shared pool is saturated? We need graceful degradation not outright fails.
[13:27] Lina: Redwood supports model-fallback chains: canary to smaller quantized variant, then to shorter-context recency model, then to a cached response. The routing policy is pluggable per route.

[14:00] Samir: Let's cover billing and reserved commitments briefly — reserved GPUs are billed monthly with a baseline commit; burst usage billed as overage. We can show sample numbers in the worksheet.

[14:20] Priya: Any compliance concerns with quantization models?
[14:24] Lina: Quantization is a model artifact; compliance concerns are about model outputs and auditability. As long as you keep evaluation artifacts and logs they're fine. For PHI, the key is where data is processed — Private or on-prem solves most regulator concerns.

[15:00] (Conversation continues; jumping ahead to specific technical clarifications)

[25:00] Lina: A concrete note on queue discipline: if you set a priority queue for clinician-interactive traffic with admission control, your effective P95 for high-priority traffic drops dramatically because low-priority jobs get preempted at admission time, not mid-inference.

[30:00] Eric: How do you measure tail latency attributed to GPU scheduling vs KV cache misses vs network?
[30:07] Lina: We instrument per-request traces — breakdown: client RTT, network egress, model forward time, kv-get times, queuing delay. Redwood Console surfaces token-level cost and per-stage latency. We'll provide sample traces so you can map observed P95 to root cause.

[35:00] Priya: On the subject of model variants, do you advise running a quantized variant in parallel for immediate fallback?
[35:06] Lina: For critical workloads yes. Keep a hot, slightly lower-quality quantized variant as fast fallback. Run continuous evaluation to ensure quality delta is acceptable.

[40:00] Monica: For the VPC setup we'll likely want an air-gapped package eventually. Any special considerations for warm pools in air-gapped?
[40:08] Samir: In air-gapped, you ship an image snapshot containing KV warm files or pre-baked cache snapshot. The orchestration then boots from that local snapshot eliminating egress at boot. That's what our private on-prem package supports.

[45:00] Eric: About queueing math — do you publish the formula you use for recommended reserved size?
[45:07] Lina: Yes, it's in the worksheet. Simplified: Recommended_reserved = ceil( (sum_over_minutes(max(0, (qps_minute * avg_tokens_minute) / tokens_sec_per_worker - burst_damping))) * safety_factor ). We also add a warmup_penalty for minutes flagged as cold_kv. The actual implementation is in the spreadsheet we'll send.

[50:00] Priya: Any pitfalls customers usually miss?
[50:05] Lina: Three common ones: 1) ignoring KV cache warmup, 2) not modeling correlated arrivals (calendar-driven spikes), and 3) assuming linear scaling with quantization without re-eval.

[55:00] Samir: Ok, wrap-up. We'll run the pilot, share the worksheet, and Lina will share bench harness. Anything else?
[55:10] Priya: Please include an example of admission-control config and priority queue settings.
[55:15] Monica: And include secure KMS flow for private deployment.

[56:00] Lina: Will do. We'll also include a short how-to for pre-warming KV snapshots inside the VPC.
[56:12] Samir: Thanks folks. We'll send the package and a calendar invite for the kickoff.

[61:50] (meeting ends)
notes: Redwood to provide cache-warmup template and admission-control configs
Pilot will use traffic replay and run three bench profiles
Prioritize clinician interactive queries with priority queues and fallback to quantized variant
